title: SQL and relational modeling
summary: Design tables, keys, relationships, and constraints, query with joins, and make concurrent mutations safe.

lessons.title: Tables, types, keys, and constraints
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of integrity of a relational row in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of integrity of a relational row.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: A table represents a set of entities of one kind; each column defines a value, each key provides identity, and each constraint rejects invalid state at the final boundary. The schema is an executable contract, not optional documentation. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: integrity of a relational row is like a workbook where every sheet has identity, entry rules, and verified references to other sheets. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

uuid gives identity independent of insertion order, while unique on slug guarantees one product URL never maps to two rows. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

not null expresses a required value; default does not replace domain validation but keeps inserts coherent when the value is truly implicit. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

Checks on cents and stock also protect scripts, imports, and future APIs that may bypass today’s form validation. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

lessons.title: Relationships and normalization
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of modeling relationships between entities in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of modeling relationships between entities.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: A one-to-many relationship places the foreign key on the many side; a many-to-many relationship becomes a junction table carrying its own attributes. Normalization stores each changing fact once, while a historical snapshot deliberately copies what must remain frozen. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: modeling relationships between entities is like a workbook where every sheet has identity, entry rules, and verified references to other sheets. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

order_items materializes the order-product relationship and carries quantity and purchased price; those attributes belong to the relationship, not the product alone. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

product_id may become null when a product is deleted, but product_name and unit_price_cents remain so the historical invoice never changes. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

ON DELETE cascade fits lines dependent on a removed order, while profiles or products often require restrict, archive, or set null based on audit needs. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

items.definition: A one-to-many relationship places the foreign key on the many side; a many-to-many relationship becomes a junction table carrying its own attributes. Normalization stores each changing fact once, while a historical snapshot deliberately copies what must remain frozen.
order_items materializes the order-product relationship and carries quantity and purchased price; those attributes belong to the relationship, not the product alone.
A controlled reference to another table’s key.
A rule the database guarantees for every write.

blocks.title: General application
blocks.text: Draw cardinalities and lifecycles, then decide whether deletion should restrict, preserve, or cascade for every relationship.

code.source:
create table order_items (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  order_id uuid not null references orders(id) on delete cascade,
  product_id uuid references products(id) on delete set null,
  product_name text not null,
  unit_price_cents integer not null check (unit_price_cents >= 0),
  quantity integer not null check (quantity > 0),
  unique (order_id, product_id)
);

blocks.text: A query describes the desired result: FROM chooses sets, JOIN relates rows, WHERE filters before aggregation, GROUP BY forms groups, and ORDER BY guarantees order. The engine then chooses an execution plan that indexes can accelerate. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: construction of a relational result is like a workbook where every sheet has identity, entry rules, and verified references to other sheets. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

INNER JOIN excludes orders without lines; LEFT JOIN would retain them with nulls, a choice driven by the domain question rather than syntax preference. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

sum computes in the database without transferring every row to the server; multiplying cents by quantity keeps integer math aligned with snapshots. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

A secondary id criterion makes order deterministic when two orders share created_at, which is required for stable pagination. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

code.source:
select
  o.id, o.created_at,
  sum(oi.unit_price_cents * oi.quantity) as subtotal_cents,
  count(oi.id) as line_count
from orders o
join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.id
where o.status = 'paid'
group by o.id, o.created_at
order by o.created_at desc, o.id desc
limit 20;

objectives: Build an accurate mental model of atomicity of a multi-table mutation.

blocks.text: A transaction creates an all-or-nothing boundary around several writes: a failure must restore the previous state. Indexes accelerate specific access patterns at the cost of space and write work, while migrations version every schema change. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: atomicity of a multi-table mutation is like a workbook where every sheet has identity, entry rules, and verified references to other sheets. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

The stock >= 2 condition merges checking and decrement into one atomic statement; zero returned rows means unavailable without negative stock. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

Creating order_items only after stock succeeds and rolling back on any exception prevents paid orders without reservation or reservations without a line. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

An index follows a frequent filter and ordering query; multiplying indexes slows INSERT/UPDATE and does not fix a query selecting too much data. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.
